profiles.meeting_scenario: A regional NHS health technology assessment unit is holding a brainstorming meeting to shape a MedtecHTA-style pilot evaluation for the OrthoNav R5, a new robotic-assisted total knee arthroplasty platform that one hospital in the region wants to introduce next financial year. The context is early scoping rather than formal appraisal: the team wants to identify what evidence, costing elements, and implementation effects should be included before drafting a fuller assessment plan. The agenda is to generate candidate approaches for handling the surgeon learning curve, defining the right comparator, capturing organizational impact, and reflecting dynamic pricing over the likely rollout period. The expected outcome is a shortlist of framing ideas and workstreams for a pilot HTA scoping note, not a final recommendation on adoption.

members.name: Dr. Hannah Price
members.role: Senior Health Economist, Regional HTA Unit
members.expertise: Economic evaluation of medical devices, service redesign costing, NICE-aligned evidence synthesis
members.background: Hannah has spent eight years producing assessments for hospital procurement and commissioning teams, with a focus on technologies whose costs change during implementation and scale-up.
members.private_state: She wants the pilot to demonstrate that the unit can operationalize MedtecHTA ideas in a way that is still manageable for a rapid regional assessment, and she is quietly worried about committing to data collection that the unit cannot sustain.
hidden_assumptions: If the team says they will model the device's 'learning phase', that naturally means a case-based curve at the surgeon level until operative time and revision-related indicators stabilize.

When clinicians mention the 'current standard pathway' for knee replacement, they usually mean the trust-wide average mix of conventional manual cases, including occasional patient-specific guides and center-to-center variation.

Organizational impact should include any hospital resource use that changes because of the device, even if those resources sit outside orthopedics, such as CT capacity, IT interfaces, and sterile services time.
A meaningful device price for HTA is the net cost to the hospital over the contract life, including service, software, and expected consumables adjustments rather than the headline capital figure.

members.name: Mr. Daniel Iqbal
members.role: Consultant Orthopedic Surgeon and Elective Surgery Innovation Lead
members.expertise: Primary knee arthroplasty, theatre implementation, surgeon training and pathway redesign
members.background: Daniel leads the elective knee program at the trust's flagship center and has previously helped introduce navigation tools and enhanced recovery protocols into routine practice.
members.private_state: He wants the discussion to produce a practical and credible assessment frame that will not make the robotic platform look artificially burdensome during early adoption, and he is sensitive to anything that could delay internal support for the business case.
hidden_assumptions: If the team refers to the device's 'learning phase', that naturally means the initial go-live period for the whole theatre pathway, measured in calendar time and team familiarity rather than surgeon case counts.

When people say 'conventional knees' or the 'standard pathway', they are talking about the straightforward jig-based technique used in his main elective center, because that is the real local benchmark in day-to-day clinical discussion.

Organizational impact mainly means the extra activities orthopedics must actively organize for rollout, such as training days, rep presence, and theatre scheduling changes, not hospital-wide infrastructure that already exists.

The commercial conversation so far is about the capital lease and per-case disposables from the orthopedic budget; service coverage and training support are usually handled separately or absorbed elsewhere unless procurement later bundles them.
If a brainstorming meeting agrees to look at pricing dynamically, that usually means reflecting how per-case costs change as volume rises, not reopening what counts as part of the price.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the device's learning phase
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree to account for the 'learning phase' in the pilot assessment.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a surgeon-level case-count learning curve, likely the first 15-20 robotic cases per operating surgeon, modeled through changes in operating time and early outcomes.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the first few months after go-live while the full theatre team settles into the pathway, regardless of how many cases each surgeon has personally completed.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both interpretations are professionally plausible and closely related, so the phrase 'learning phase' feels precise enough in a brainstorming context; each assumes the other is simply using ordinary implementation language.

misalignment_points.topic: Which care pathway is the comparator
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say the pilot should compare the robot against the 'current standard pathway' or 'conventional knees'.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the trust-wide baseline pathway across all sites, including the mixed real-world average of manual instrumentation and some patient-specific guides in selected cases.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the standard jig-based manual technique used at his own elective hub, which he treats as the obvious local comparator.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrases 'current standard pathway' and 'conventional knees' normally signal agreement, and neither person expects that such a familiar comparator label hides site-level variation significant enough to restate during an initial ideation meeting.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree the assessment should include 'organizational impact'.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 includes downstream CT scheduling, image transfer and IT integration work, sterile services handling, theatre downtime for software updates, and procurement administration in addition to direct orthopedic workflow changes.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 includes only rollout burdens directly experienced by the orthopedic service, such as surgeon and scrub training, proctoring sessions, and altered theatre lists during early use.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In HTA language, 'organizational impact' sounds broad but self-explanatory, and in a cooperative brainstorming exchange both assume they are merely adding examples inside the same umbrella rather than drawing different boundaries around it.

misalignment_points.topic: What the dynamic device price already includes
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree to model the robot's 'price trajectory over the contract life'.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 presupposes this means the all-in net hospital price after procurement negotiation, including service cover, software updates, and expected consumables terms over several years.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 presupposes this means the capital lease plus changing per-case disposable costs, while service support, training, and some implementation support sit outside the price line unless later negotiated in.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are accustomed to hearing vendors and managers use 'price' loosely, and because the meeting is only for idea generation, neither thinks it necessary to unpack which cost components are already assumed to be bundled.

turns.inner_thought: I need to keep this pilot tight enough for a rapid regional HTA, but still show we can do something recognizably MedtecHTA. So the frame should cover the learning phase in a way we can model from case-level data, use the current standard pathway as the trust-wide real-world baseline rather than an idealized single-site comparator, include organizational impact across the hospital where the robot changes resource use, and reflect the robot's price trajectory over the contract life as the net hospital cost rather than a sticker price. If I let this sprawl into bespoke data collection everywhere, we'll never deliver it.
turns.utterance: Thanks, Daniel. I thought today we could keep this at scoping level and try to pin down a sensible MedtecHTA-style frame for the OrthoNav R5. For me, the key is to capture the learning phase, the current standard pathway, organizational impact, and the robot's price trajectory over the contract life, but do it in a way that's proportionate for a pilot rather than a full formal appraisal.

turns.inner_thought: That sounds workable. What matters most locally is that the assessment doesn't make the platform look artificially poor just because the first few months are always messy when a new theatre process goes live. If we can show what performance looks like once the whole team is through the learning phase, the business case will be much easier to defend internally.
turns.utterance: Yes, that makes sense. From the elective knee side, the real value of the pilot will be showing what the system looks like once we've got through the learning phase and the service is running in a more settled way.

turns.inner_thought: Good, we're aligned on needing a learning-phase adjustment. I should steer this toward something we can represent analytically: early-case effects for each operating surgeon, then a steadier state once operative time and revision-related indicators settle. I won't over-specify that now; 'track early-case effects' will be enough.
turns.utterance: Agreed. One option for the pilot would be to represent the learning phase explicitly, so we track early-case effects and then separate those from the steadier pattern later on. That at least stops the first tranche of activity being blended into the rest as though nothing changes.

turns.inner_thought: Exactly. In practice the meaningful disruption is in the first few months after go-live: list flow, who knows where to stand, how the trays move, and how much rep support is needed. That's where organizational impact really bites for us, and it isn't mainly about how many cases any one surgeon has done. I can keep it general and he'll hear a sensible implementation point.
turns.utterance: Yes, and I think the key period to think about is that first stretch after go-live, because that's when list flow, scrub familiarity, and rep support are all most live. If the pilot can reflect that part of the learning phase properly, it will feel much more credible.

turns.inner_thought: Now comparator. For commissioners, the credible baseline is the current standard pathway across the trust, with all the ordinary variation that's already in the system, including occasional patient-specific guides. If I say 'across the trust' plainly enough, that should anchor the dataset without getting into methodological weeds.
turns.utterance: On the comparator, my instinct is that we should anchor the pilot against the current standard pathway across the trust, so we're reflecting the baseline that commissioners are actually used to seeing rather than something too selective.

turns.inner_thought: Fine by me. In practical terms that means conventional knees at the elective hub, because that's what everyone here means when they talk about the standard pathway day to day. It's the cleanest benchmark and avoids muddying the picture with variation from elsewhere.
turns.utterance: Yes, I agree with that. Conventional knees give us a clean benchmark, particularly at the elective hub, because that's the pathway the surgeons and theatre teams are comparing themselves against all the time.

turns.inner_thought: I should widen the organizational impact list now so it doesn't get reduced to theatre inconvenience. For this kind of device we need to capture CT scheduling, image transfer and interfaces, sterile services handling, downtime for software updates, and other knock-on resource use as well as direct orthopedic training. I'll mention examples but keep them under the umbrella term.
turns.utterance: In terms of organizational impact, I think the pilot should at least map a few categories rather than just note that there is one. So alongside theatre training and list changes, we could note things like imaging requirements, setup around image transfer, sterile services handling, and any downtime issues if they arise.

turns.inner_thought: Those other items may exist in the background, but the practical organizational impact for us is really protected training lists, proctoring, rep presence, and some short-term inefficiency while the team settles. I don't want this to become a giant hospital-wide burden inventory that scares people off before we've even started.
turns.utterance: That sounds reasonable. From the service side, I suspect the main organizational impact we'll actually feel will be protected training lists, proctoring days, and a bit of short-term theatre inefficiency while everything settles down.

turns.inner_thought: Now the pricing issue. I need to signal that we should model contract-life cost properly, not just cite the capital headline. If service cover, software, and consumables terms evolve over time, the price trajectory over the contract life needs to reflect that all-in pattern. I'll phrase it broadly so he doesn't think I'm reopening procurement detail at this stage.
turns.utterance: On costing, I'd be keen for us to reflect the robot's price trajectory over the contract life rather than reduce it to a single upfront number. Especially with these technologies, the picture can shift as the arrangement matures and volume changes, so a dynamic view would be more useful.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, exactly: the lease is fixed, and once volume comes up the per-case disposables should look better, so the price trajectory over the contract life ought to improve after year one. I don't need to drag service support and training into the price line unless procurement does that later; for now the commercial story is simple enough.
turns.utterance: I think that's right. If we look at the price trajectory over the contract life, it should look more representative than any year-zero figure, because the per-case position is likely to improve once activity rises after the first year.

turns.inner_thought: Good. I have enough to draft a concise scoping note: learning phase, conventional comparator, organizational impact, and contract-life costing. Later I'll need to make these operational in my own terms, but for now this sounds like consensus and keeps the scope manageable.
turns.utterance: That's helpful. What I'll do is draft a one-page scoping note built around those four headings: the learning phase, the conventional comparator, organizational impact, and contract-life costing. Then we can see where we need light-touch evidence gathering versus anything more involved.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. I'll send examples from our hub showing how rollout felt in practice and what our usual conventional pathway looks like. That should help keep the assessment grounded in the real implementation story without overcomplicating it.
turns.utterance: That framing sounds right to me. I'm happy to send across a few examples from the elective hub that illustrate the rollout experience and the usual conventional pathway, so you've got something concrete to work from when you put the note together.
